identity.title: Does Stochastic Gradient really succeed for bandits?

problem.claim: Characterize the regret regimes of the Stochastic Gradient Bandit policy as a function of its learning rate.

gap.claim: It remains unclear whether logarithmic regret extends beyond sufficiently small learning rates.

contributions.claim: For two-armed bandits, identifies a gap-dependent threshold separating logarithmic-regret behavior on all instances from possible polynomial regret on some instances.
Shows that for general K-armed bandits, the learning rate must scale inversely with K to avoid polynomial regret.
Introduces techniques for deriving regret upper bounds for Stochastic Gradient Bandit policies.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they introduce novel techniques for Stochastic Gradient Bandit regret upper bounds.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that, for two-armed bandits, learning rates below a sharp sub-optimality-gap-scaled threshold yield logarithmic regret on all instances, whereas rates above it can yield polynomial regret on some instances.
The authors report that avoiding polynomial regret in general K-armed bandits requires inverse-K learning-rate scaling.

narrative_sequence.summary: Earlier work is described as establishing asymptotic convergence with a constant learning rate and logarithmic regret for sufficiently small rates.
The abstract identifies uncertainty about logarithmic regret beyond small learning rates.
A gap-dependent threshold is reported for two-armed bandits, separating all-instance logarithmic regret from possible polynomial regret on some instances.
For K arms, inverse-K scaling is reported as necessary to avoid polynomial regret, alongside techniques intended to support future theory.

source_observation.claim: The paper organizes its main two-armed result around a sharp threshold whose scale depends on the sub-optimality gap, and explicitly connects that threshold to the need to know or estimate the gap.

lessons.interpretation: Parameter-regime boundaries can make theoretical guarantees more actionable than a single undifferentiated rate statement.
lessons.application: When presenting a learning-rate guarantee, state the governing instance parameter, identify the boundary between regret regimes, and explain whether that parameter must be known or estimated.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when no meaningful instance parameter or regime transition has been established.

unknowns: The abstract does not give the threshold's exact formula or constants.
It does not specify how the sub-optimality gap could be estimated, nor the conditions and proof details behind the reported bounds.
“Some instances” with polynomial regret are not characterized in the abstract.
